- If model consistently overestimates prices in early forecast horizon (e.g., first 5–10 days), reduce initial forecast values by 2–5% to account for mean reversion or market correction.
- If true outcome shows sharp spikes (e.g., >10% above recent mean), model tends to overreact — cap forecast slope after spike to avoid overshoot.
- When sentiment history is flat (all 0.00), model should not assume sentiment-driven momentum — treat as neutral baseline, avoid extrapolation.
- If true outcome deviates significantly from historical mean (e.g., >15% above/below), adjust forecast mean by subtracting 1–3 standard deviations to reflect volatility.
- For 30-day forecasts, if model shows monotonic rise or fall without reversal, check for lag — introduce slight downward bias in later days if prior days show upward trend.
- If model forecast is consistently higher than true outcome across multiple days, apply a “price floor” correction: if forecast > true outcome by >5%, reduce forecast by 1–3% per day to align with observed downward drift.
- If sentiment history is non-zero (even if small), model should adjust forecast to reflect sentiment bias — e.g., if sentiment >0.2, add 1–2% to forecast; if < -0.2, subtract 1–2%.
